query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy protective coatings, a fine-grained microstructure enhances wear resistance by promoting the rapid formation of a continuous, adherent, and mechanically robust friction-induced oxide (tribolayer), which acts as a barrier to adhesive and abrasive wear, in contrast to coarse-grained structures that develop unstable, cracked oxide layers leading to higher wear rates.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy coating (e.g., equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi) deposited with an identical chemical composition but processed into two distinct initial microstructures: one with a fine-grained (submicron/nanocrystalline) structure and one with a coarse-grained (tens of microns) structure.
generation.intervention: Application of a controlled thermomechanical processing step (e.g., rapid cooling or specific annealing protocols) to refine the grain size of the coating. Key parameters such as cooling rate and annealing time are adjusted to produce a fine-grained microstructure, while a baseline sample is processed under conditions that favor coarse grains.
generation.conditions: Wear testing using pin-on-disk experiments performed under identical sliding conditions (constant load, speed, and ambient atmosphere) at room temperature and moderate elevated temperatures. The tests must provide sufficient frictional heating to induce oxide formation without causing melting or severe degradation.
generation.structural_mediator: The grain size – which governs the density of grain boundaries and the kinetics of oxide nucleation and growth during sliding contact.
generation.mechanism: Fine grains provide an increased density of active sites (grain boundaries) that promote rapid and uniform oxidation under frictional heating. This results in a continuous, adherent, and mechanically resilient tribolayer that reduces direct metal-to-metal contact and limits plastic deformation. In contrast, a coarse-grained microstructure leads to localized plasticity and uneven oxidation, causing the protective oxide layer to crack and spall under repeated loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical wear testing conditions, fine-grained HEA coatings will demonstrate significantly lower friction coefficients (e.g., reduced by approximately 20–30%) and reduced specific wear rates compared to their coarse-grained counterparts. Post-test microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM, EDS) will show intact, continuous oxide or tribolayers in fine-grained samples, whereas coarse-grained coatings will exhibit discontinuous, cracked oxide layers.
generation.baseline: The coarse-grained HEA coating produced by a slower cooling process or minimal post-processing, which is expected to form less continuous and more fragmented oxide layers during wear, leading to higher friction and wear rates.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under conditions where frictional heating is sufficient to trigger oxide formation (moderate to high sliding loads and speeds in an atmospheric environment) but may be less applicable in extreme environments (e.g., ultrahigh vacuum) where oxidation is inhibited.
generation.uncertainty: Variability in ambient oxygen concentration, potential residual stresses from processing, and the influence of any secondary phases or compositional inhomogeneities not solely controlled by grain size may introduce deviations from the expected tribolayer behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeMnNi HEA coatings with identical compositions but distinct grain sizes (fine-grained and coarse-grained) via controlled thermomechanical processing. Subject both sets to standardized pin-on-disk wear tests under identical ambient conditions at both room temperature and moderate elevated temperatures.
measurements: Friction coefficient recorded continuously during sliding
Wear rate determined by mass loss or volume loss measurements
Surface characterization via SEM and EDS to assess oxide/tribolayer continuity and morphology
Grain size analysis before and after wear using TEM or EBSD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the fine-grained coatings do not show a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the coarse-grained coatings, or if the oxide layer on the fine-grained sample is not more continuous and adherent (e.g., if both samples display similar oxide spallation and cracking), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Thus, if cooperative heterostructures capable of releasing frictional stress in stages are configured in the alloy, it is expected to suppress the sliding-induced deformation. In contrast, upon wear at high temperatures (≥600 °C), the wear behavior of the material becomes quite complex, stemming from the prevalence of surface adhesion and tribo-oxidation at the friction interface [,]. High-temperature sliding tends to soften the metallic surface that endows the near-surface material susceptible to chemical instability caused by counterbody materials or environmental oxygen, triggering severe delamination wear and composition segregation at the friction interface that exacerbates wear [,]. Materials become more dependent on tribochemical protection upon high-temperature wear due to deterioration in stiffness [,]. Tribo-oxidation may promote the formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) consisting of various nanocrystalline (NC) oxides on the worn surface, which assists in enhancing the friction interface while providing solid lubrication [,,]. Since their discovery in 2004,, high entropy alloys (HEAs) have been extensively investigated and shown to exhibit remarkable thermomechanical properties,. Studies of grain-size dependent mechanical behavior are limited,, however, especially in the regime of ultra-nanocrystalline grain size where softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) occurs. Recent work has also shown that these alloys are ideally suited for processing using laser-based additive manufacturing techniques, as they exhibit high phase stability and derive much of their strength from thermal history-insensitive mechanisms like solution strengthening. While recent publications have presented experimental evidence of low friction or high wear resistance (but typically not both) with HEAs, they were performed in environments where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide surface films was prevalent. These phenomena can greatly impact strength and deformation/wear resistance. This work studied an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy that was manufactured using a laser-based consolidation additive manufacturing process. We showed that low friction and high wear resistance are achievable with bare high entropy alloys in inert environments. These characteristics are linked to the shear-induced formation of a highly refined, near-amorphous surface film that exhibits inverse Hall-Petch behavior. The detrimental role of environments, specifically those that result in oxidation, was mitigated by tribological testing in a UHV environment. A newly proposed amorphization model was used to accurately predict the grain size-dependent shear strength, and thus friction coefficient.

AbstractThe effect and mechanism of grain sizes on the tribological behavior of CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy (HEA) were studied by friction experiments and wear morphology analysis. Under normal low load and low sliding speed, the primary wear mechanism of the HEA samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the samples are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. The oxide layer formed under the action of friction heat of the coarse grain (CG) sample is easy to break due to the softening of the CG. With the increase of normal load and sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the HEA samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation. The oxide layer of CG sample has many cracks, and the worn surface also has plastic deformation, which leads to the increase of friction coefficient and specific wear rate and the decrease of wear resistance. Therefore, the fine grain size HEA sample has better wear resistance than the CG sample due to its high surface strength.Keywords: high entropy alloy, grain size, tribological behavior, wear mechanism

In the present study, the tribological properties of different grain sizes CoCrFeMnNi HEAs were systematically analyzed based on sliding experiments and worn surface morphology characterization under different sliding speeds and normal loads. The results can be summarized as follows: Under the normal low load and low sliding speed, the main wear mechanism of FG and CG samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. However, the material of CG is easy to soften under the action of friction heat during high sliding speed, and the oxide layer formed is easy to fracture. Under the normal high load, the wear mechanisms of FG and CG samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation with the increase of sliding speed. The oxidation layer formed on CG sample has many cracks, and the wear surface of CG sample also has plastic deformation, resulting in an increase in friction coefficient and specific wear rate and a decrease in wear resistance. Therefore, under high load and low load, FG sample has good wear resistance due to its high surface strength.

papers.title: Effect of Grain Size on the Tribological Behavior of CoCrFeMnNi High Entropy Alloy.
papers.approach: Sliding friction experiments under varied loads and speeds combined with wear morphology analysis.
papers.findings: Fine-grained samples exhibited lower friction coefficients and wear rates than coarse-grained samples, due to enhanced surface strength and a more stable, less cracked oxide layer. In contrast, coarse grains softened under friction heat leading to brittle, cracked oxide layers and higher wear.
papers.mechanism: Grain size governs wear performance via its influence on the stability and integrity of friction-induced oxide layers and resistance to plastic deformation; coarse grains are prone to softening and oxide cracking, promoting adhesive and oxidative wear.

papers.title: Remarkable Wear Resistance in a Complex Concentrated Alloy with Nanohierarchical Architecture and Composition Undulation.
papers.approach: Fabrication of alloys with engineered nanohierarchical architecture and composition undulation; comparison of tribological responses under room and elevated temperature sliding.
papers.findings: The formation of gradient nanocrystalline layers and self-organized glaze layers led to significantly reduced wear, especially at high temperatures where a stable tribo-layer assisted in resisting elastic–plastic deformation.
papers.mechanism: A cooperative heterostructure allows staged stress release via in situ formation of protective, lubricious tribo-layers and gradient-recrystallized zones that accommodate strain gradients during sliding.

papers.title: Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA fabricated by laser-based additive manufacturing
papers.approach: Friction and wear experiments in ultra-high vacuum (UHV) to eliminate oxidation effects, combined with electron microscopy grain size measurements and a dynamic amorphization model.
papers.findings: Extremely low friction coefficients (~0.3) and very low wear rates were achieved, attributed to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline, near-surface layer arising from shear-induced grain refinement.
papers.mechanism: Dynamic grain refinement leads to an inverse Hall-Petch (softening) effect that reduces surface shear strength and friction, setting a lower bound for friction coefficients in an inert environment.

papers.title: High Hardness and Wear Resistance in AlCrFeNiV High-Entropy Alloy Induced by Dual-Phase Body-Centered Cubic Coupling Effects.
papers.system: AlCrFeNiV HEA with dual BCC phases
papers.approach: Synthesis via high-energy ball milling and spark plasma sintering followed by dry wear tests against an Al2O3 counter-body; detailed microstructural and mechanical analysis.
papers.findings: The alloy exhibited ultrahigh hardness (over 1076 HV0.5) and excellent wear resistance, correlated with the presence of two BCC phases that interact to arrest dislocation motion and inhibit interfacial cracking.
papers.mechanism: Interfacial coupling between dual BCC phases enhances work hardening and resists crack initiation, while also promoting the local formation of a dense oxide layer that contributes to wear protection.

papers.title: Effects of W Alloying on the Lattice Distortion and Wear Behavior of Laser Cladding AlCoCrFeNiWₓ High-Entropy Alloy Coatings.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNiWₓ HEA coatings on hot working die steel
papers.approach: Laser cladding coatings with varying tungsten content, followed by high-temperature friction and wear testing, microstructural characterization and XAFS analysis.
papers.findings: W addition resulted in the formation of W-rich intermetallic compounds and increased lattice distortion, significantly improving high-temperature wear resistance despite fluctuations in friction coefficient due to oxide layer dynamics.
papers.mechanism: Increased lattice distortion and second-phase strengthening due to tungsten incorporation enhance the resistance to dynamic recrystallization and plastic deformation during high-temperature wear, thereby stabilizing the microstructure.

established: Grain size and microstructural refinement (including dynamic shear-induced amorphization) play a critical role in determining friction coefficient and wear rate.
Formation and stability of oxide and tribo-layers are essential for wear resistance under sliding conditions.
Dual-phase or heterostructured architectures enhance mechanical strength and resist plastic deformation.

approaches_tried.approach: Controlling grain size (fine vs. coarse) through processing methods
approaches_tried.outcome: Fine-grained structures exhibited better wear resistance and lower friction, while coarse grains led to softening and oxide layer rupture.

approaches_tried.approach: Engineering nanohierarchical and compositionally undulated heterostructures
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved formation of protective glaze and gradient tribo-layers with higher wear resistance, particularly at elevated temperatures.

approaches_tried.approach: Utilizing additive manufacturing under inert conditions to exploit inverse Hall-Petch behavior
approaches_tried.outcome: Achieved extremely low friction coefficients and low wear rates via dynamic surface grain refinement.

approaches_tried.approach: Alloying additions (e.g., tungsten, titanium) to induce lattice distortion and form reinforcing intermetallic phases
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced high-temperature wear behavior and increased hardness by promoting second-phase strengthening.

mechanisms: Grain refinement and dynamic amorphization leading to reduced shear strength (inverse Hall-Petch effect)
Formation of stable, protective oxide/tribo-layers that reduce direct contact and adhesive wear
Dual-phase interfacial coupling and lattice distortion enhancing work hardening and resistance to crack propagation
disagreements: Some studies attribute wear improvements primarily to oxide layer stability and its protective effects, while others emphasize dynamic grain refinement and inverse Hall-Petch softening as the dominant factor.
The role of high-temperature oxidation varies; certain works report beneficial glaze layer formation, whereas others indicate that oxidation can lead to brittle oxide spallation and increased wear.
open_questions: How do engineered microstructural features (grain size, dual-phase boundaries, heterostructures) interact under complex, varying thermal and mechanical loads?
What are the quantitative limits of the inverse Hall-Petch regime across different HEA systems during wear?
How does the evolution of protective oxide layers under real-world service conditions correlate with underlying microstructural stability?
Can the balance between dynamic softening and hardening be optimized universally for high-entropy alloy coatings?
opportunities: Investigate combined alloying strategies (e.g., simultaneous W and Ti additions) with controlled grain refinement to fine-tune oxide layer formation and mechanical properties.
Perform in situ high-temperature tribological testing to decouple oxidation effects from mechanical deformation mechanisms.
Develop scalable additive manufacturing routes that exploit nanohierarchical architectures and controlled compositional undulations for optimized wear resistance.
Explore systematic comparisons in inert versus oxidative environments to delineate the competing roles of inverse Hall-Petch behavior and tribo-oxidation in wear performance.

directions.direction: Altering the alloy composition to modify the oxide‐forming elements and hence the protective tribolayer chemistry.
directions.assessment: This approach directly influences the chemical potential for oxide formation but adds complexity because composition changes may also affect bulk mechanical properties. The mechanism is chemically driven and less isolated from other variables.

directions.direction: Using different thermomechanical processing routes to control grain size, thereby modifying the evolution and stability of friction‐induced oxide/tribo-layers.
directions.assessment: This strategy directly tests how microstructural refinement impacts wear performance through the mediating effect on oxide formation at the sliding interface. It is supported by evidence showing that fine-grained HEAs form more continuous and crack‐resistant oxide layers (e.g., PMC9960858::web::000 and PMC9960858::web::021) and is highly feasible in a controlled experimental setup.

directions.direction: Applying surface treatments such as laser cladding parameter adjustments or shot peening to modify the top surface microtexture and improve tribo-layer adhesion.
directions.assessment: While this direction can improve surface integrity and oxide adherence, it may also introduce residual stresses and roughness effects that complicate the isolated study of the underlying mechanism governing wear.

directions.direction: Performing in situ high-temperature tribological testing with real-time monitoring of oxide layer evolution by advanced microscopy.
directions.assessment: This method gives direct insight into how the oxide layers form and deform under wear conditions. However, such experiments are technically demanding and require specialized equipment, potentially limiting throughput and isolating the effect of microstructural features.

directions.direction: Developing atomistic or continuum-level simulations to investigate how grain boundaries and dynamic recrystallization govern the formation of protective tribolayers during sliding.
directions.assessment: Model-based approaches offer deep mechanistic insights at the atomic scale but require subsequent experimental validation. They are valuable as a complementary method yet may miss macroscopic and environmental complexities inherent in wear processes.

choice.direction: Using different thermomechanical processing routes to control grain size, thereby modifying the evolution and stability of friction‐induced oxide/tribo-layers
choice.why: This approach directly tests the hypothesis that microstructural refinement (i.e., reducing grain size) improves the formation and stability of a continuous oxide or tribolayer during wear. It isolates a single variable that has been repeatedly implicated in lowering wear rates (see PMC9960858::web::000 and PMC9960858::web::021) and is both feasible and mechanistically informative.
